## [2026-10-26](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-26.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32951>)

This study traces some reinforcement-learning instability to when inference and training implementations round intermediate values, then aligns selected training operations while retaining BF16 model tensors. The tested Qwen-family runs remain stable without bitwise agreement across the whole stack, offering a targeted alternative to rebuilding the entire training and inference pipeline.

**Published:** 2026-10-23 · **First seen:** 2026-10-26T10:03:32.681+00:00 · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Numerical Stability, BF16, Reinforcement Learning

**Public availability:** 2026-10-26T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/new>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32951v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3-9 and Appendices A-D inspect fused/eager rounding, fixed-objective controls and four Qwen-family models on math RL. Keeping training RoPE-path intermediates in FP32 until BF16 outputs prevents observed collapse; all-three-region alignment also works. Table 4 reports 0.90-2.04% RoPE-only forward/backward overhead on three models, excluding rollout and optimizer updates. Monday October 26 batch plus official schedule support inferred 00:00 UTC announcement; original Friday submission date retained. No separate author code was verified.

**Limitations:** Two math datasets and one architectural family; no multi-seed confidence claim or universal stability guarantee. Other kernels/objective stay fixed; remaining numerical mismatch is nonzero. The overhead microbenchmark excludes major RL costs and cannot establish end-to-end speedup.

## [2026-10-23](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-23.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31642>)

The paper rewrites softmax and cross-entropy computations to preserve small gradients that ordinary floating-point formulations can erase or corrupt. Correcting high-confidence rounding and near-identical teacher–student cancellation prevents training spikes and distillation drift in controlled small-model experiments, providing a diagnostic and implementation fix for sensitive optimization regimes.

**Published:** 2026-10-22 · **First seen:** 2026-10-23T10:02:54.788Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Numerical Precision, Training Stability, Cross-Entropy, Distillation

**Public availability:** 2026-10-23T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Pinned v1 full ten-page PDF and HTML, Sections 1–8, Equations 1–11, Table 1, all experimental figures and inline JAX implementations inspected. Standard overflow-safe softmax can still round the confident target probability to one while leaving positive non-target gradients, breaking the exact zero-sum gradient identity; the paper reformulates the target/non-target computation using a stable margin and softplus. A separate logits-aware distillation construction uses log1p/expm1 and a projected custom gradient to preserve small teacher–student differences instead of subtracting independently rounded probabilities. This second construction requires teacher logits, not only already-rounded target probabilities. The hard-target precision cliffs are approximately margin 5.5 in bfloat16, 16.6 in float32 and 36.7 in float64; casting up delays the cliff. Controlled grokking experiments include one-layer Transformers and two-layer MLPs on modular arithmetic. The principal modular-addition experiment uses a one-layer width-64 Transformer, modulus 31, a 50% training split and 10,000 full-batch AdamW epochs. Table 1 sweeps three precisions and three Adam epsilon values over five seeds; at float32 and epsilon 1e-8, the fixed formulation reports 100.0% mean test accuracy versus 94.3% for standard cross-entropy. The distillation diagnostic begins with a student identical to an already-correct modular-arithmetic teacher, uses temperature 4, 2,000 Adam steps and three seeds, and demonstrates drift from numerical cancellation rather than useful learning from a stronger teacher. Prior work already identified collapse/slingshot behavior and proposed mitigations; the contribution is the direct stable formulation and joint numerical/optimization analysis, not the first observation of all such failures. Original receipt October 22 17:54:56 UTC retained. The original Friday October 23 cs.LG new-submission batch and official Eastern-time schedule imply paper announcement October 23 00:00 UTC. No earlier release of this complete paper/formulation was found in the bounded exact-title/author-artifact search; negative search is not proof of absence. The inspected primary paper includes implementations, but no separate author code/project release was verified.

**Limitations:** Evidence is controlled small-model arithmetic/grokking and near-identical-network distillation, not a demonstrated improvement in ordinary large-scale LLM training or downstream language capability. The authors explicitly note that the extreme confidence and near-zero teacher–student gaps may be uncommon in standard large-scale regimes. Results across precisions and optimizer epsilon settings do not establish a universal accuracy gain or an optimizer-independent training guarantee. The distillation fix needs logits and custom gradient handling, so it is not automatically a drop-in change for every fused kernel or probability-only interface. No LLM-scale throughput/latency benchmark or independent reproduction was verified.

## [2026-10-22](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-22.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29348>)

Controlled experiments show that a data-mixture schedule can help or hurt mid-training depending on when the learning rate decays, even when total compute and target-data tokens are fixed. Dense and mixture-of-experts experiments favor keeping the rate high after target data first appears and using a short final cooldown to lower target-domain validation loss, giving recipe designers a reason to tune the two schedules together.

**Published:** 2026-10-21 · **First seen:** 2026-10-22T10:07:41.810Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Data Mixtures, Learning Rate Schedules, Mid-training, Mixture of Experts

**Public availability:** 2026-10-22T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.29348v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Pinned v1 Sections 2–4 and relevant setup, repeat-run, data-schedule and cooldown appendices inspected. The study holds continuation compute and mid-training token budget fixed while varying the target-data fraction over time and the learning-rate schedule, across over 250 runs with a 630M dense model and a 2.99B-total-parameter MoE model (454M active non-embedding parameters plus embeddings). The dense model continues for 20.97152B tokens after 200B DCLM pretraining; the MoE main study uses 4B or 10B continuation tokens after 40B pretraining. FineMath is the principal target corpus, with code-data checks as well. Two-stage jumps and zero-then-linear ramps interact differently with constant learning rates and full- or matching-window decay: earlier mixing can help under full decay but lose its advantage under a constant rate. Across 19 tested cooldown sweeps, the best tested decay spans 10–40% of the mid-training window, rather than necessarily beginning when target data first appears. A ramp can have twice the mid-training window at the same target-token budget, so fractional cooldowns must also be compared in absolute steps. For example, the dense 25%-budget two-stage configuration reaches target validation cross-entropy 1.4275 with a 40% cooldown versus 1.4717 with constant learning rate and 1.4475 with decay over the matching mid-training range. These are configured-tokenizer loss units, not downstream accuracy. Selected configurations are repeated with three data-stream/order replicates sharing the same pretrained checkpoint; most sweeps have one run. Fresh optimizer state, no continuation warmup, and the within-family optimizer settings are held fixed. The original October 21 receipt (07:42:20 UTC) is retained. The paper appears in the original October 22 new-submission batch; October 22 00:00 UTC availability is inferred from that dated batch and the official Eastern-time announcement schedule. No earlier primary release was found in the bounded title/artifact search, which does not prove absence of one. The paper cites prior curriculum and schedule studies; the contribution is its controlled budget comparisons and recipe evidence, not the first observation that data and optimization interact.

**Limitations:** Evidence concerns target-domain validation loss at these model/data scales, not established downstream capability gains or a universal optimum. Pretraining loss can trade off against target loss. Only a few configurations have data-order repeats, and they share one pretrained checkpoint; close loss differences are not automatically statistically significant. The dense and MoE families have different tokenizers and optimizer details, so absolute losses are not directly comparable across families. The noisy-quadratic/SGD analysis explains the interaction under assumptions rather than proving the best schedule for Transformers. The 10–40% cooldown range is the best among tested choices, not a universal rule. No author implementation/project release was verified from the inspected primary source, and no independent reproduction was performed.

## [2026-10-09](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-09.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575>)

Elastic Expert Routing varies the number of active experts around the deployment budget during training, giving experts just beyond the usual cutoff occasional task-loss feedback. It improves the tested MoE models while retaining ordinary fixed top-k inference, providing a training intervention that preserves the serving architecture.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-09T10:03:31Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Mixture of Experts, Routing, Pretraining

**Public availability:** 2026-10-09T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/new>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. A 6–10 expert schedule centered on eight improves nine-task SFT averages by 0.84 points on OLMoE and 2.02 on Qwen3-30B-A3B; 1.42B-model pretraining improves its separate task average by 1.6 points. Original v1: 2026-10-08T09:31:19Z; October 9 new-submission batch verified.

**Limitations:** Matched expected expert FLOPs do not imply equal runtime: the preferred schedule costs about 3–5% more per SFT iteration. From-scratch evidence covers 26.25B tokens at moderate scale; results do not establish gains at frontier pretraining scale. No author implementation was verified.

## [2026-10-06](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-06.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [LightMTP: Lightweight Latent Multi-Token Prediction](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06031>)

LightMTP adds a small auxiliary head that predicts the model's own future intermediate hidden states, using stopped-gradient targets from the same training pass alongside next-token prediction. The head is discarded at inference, offering an inexpensive way to encourage future-aware representations and improve some structured reasoning tasks without changing ordinary decoding.

**Published:** 2026-10-05 · **First seen:** 2026-10-06T10:03:05Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Pretraining, Multi-Token Prediction, Latent Targets

**Public availability:** 2026-10-06T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06031>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Experiments cover 286M–1.4B decoders and multiple seeds. Countdown accuracy rises from 46.4% for next-token training to 56.7% for a LightMTP variant; the main 24-layer heads add 0.3–0.9% parameters. Original submission: 2026-10-05T09:30:30Z; October 6's listing establishes the later 00:00Z public batch inside the main window.

**Limitations:** General-language aggregate results remain near the next-token baseline, and a linear token-prediction baseline scores higher on Countdown. Training budgets grow with head size and are not matched for tokens or compute; small parameter overhead is not zero training cost. Some headline GSM8K results use a relaxed matching metric. No author implementation was verified.

## [2026-09-30](../../../reports/2026/09/2026-09-30.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38149>)

LIFT trains language models to carry a latent state across generated tokens, using a teacher's next-token distributions to supervise this feedback channel while preserving parallel pretraining. Its controlled language-modeling and procedural-task gains suggest a way to improve learning efficiency and state tracking without expressing every intermediate computation as text.

**Published:** 2026-09-29 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T10:04:44Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Pretraining, Latent Reasoning, Teacher Supervision

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3-5 and Appendix F provide architecture, ablations, and token/compute comparisons at 135M, 350M, and 1B non-embedding parameters; compute matching includes teacher forward passes. The main three-scale experiment reports 5-5.5% lower perplexity at matched tokens. The arXiv v1 submission was 2026-09-29T17:57:40Z, within the daily interval.

**Limitations:** Only the smallest language-model scale has three training seeds; larger runs have one. Main evaluations use sequential prompt processing, while parallel prefill trades extra passes for quality; results are not uniformly better than vanilla Transformers across every compute-matched setting.

## [2026-09-29 — Landscape baseline](../../../landscape/2026-09-29.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534>)

Kimi K2 introduces MuonClip, which adds query/key weight clipping to Muon so that attention logits remain controlled during large-scale mixture-of-experts training. It is a practical optimization reference because it links a specific instability mechanism to an intervention used in a trillion-parameter training run.

**Published:** 2025-07-28 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T04:09:33Z · **Novelty:** baseline · **Tags:** Muon, Optimization, Training Stability, MoE

**Positioning:** established-method

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534>) · [Project](<https://github.com/MoonshotAI/Kimi-K2>)

**Evidence:** technical-report; full-text. The optimizer algorithm, mid-scale instability experiment, and Appendix D ablations accompany the authors' report of training on 15.5 trillion tokens without observed loss spikes.

**Limitations:** This is an established recipe component, not a current model ranking; the trillion-parameter evidence is author-reported, and the intervention needs attention-specific adaptation and threshold choices.
